doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Vocal inflection, early R&B tastes and jazz on parents' records
summary: He liked R&B singers, Doris Day with Les Brown and Basie's One O'Clock Jump on a sampler, and rejected the Beatles as too dumb.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: You’ve mentioned the vocal connection. People, instrumentalists, using vocal — loss for words here — vocal inflections.
It seems very important to you.

It was a way of connecting. I was not also taken with pop vocal music. It just didn’t — I liked the rhythm & blues sound, I don’t know why, the hoarseness maybe of some of the masculine baritone singers. I remember “Duke of Earl” very well, or “Alley-Oop” the Coasters. These are the kinds of songs that I liked. I was not into the ballads. I didn’t care about Johnny Mathis that was hot at the time. I don’t think I had been exposed to Jackie Wilson then. One of the first jazz vocals that I really remember, and this is again on my © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

parents’ records, was Doris Day singing “Sentimental Journey” with Les Brown. And I really liked that. And it was on a sampler. Lucky Strike put out some sort of “This is Jazz” LP. And it also had Count Basie’s “One O’clock Jump” on it which I liked a lot. And that sort of mystified me because it didn’t have a melody at the beginning.

And so that gave me a sense that there was a way of arriving at something in a different structure, I mean that’s okay? All right. I can buy that then. And I think this was one of my intellectual snobbery, and rock & roll and pop music just didn’t seem, I don’t know, sophisticated enough or interesting, and the singing, especially twelve, thirteen, when I was twelve and thirteen was when the Beatles came on the scene. And they were singing yeah-yeah-yeah and I was like no-no-no. You know, this is just too dumb. I’m more sophisticated than that. I read Hemingway or something.
